_comment: Registration for scripts/check-doc-helper-flags.py (issue #1835).
WHY THIS GATE NEEDS A COMMITTED CASE (ADR 0008): it is a gate that lets work
THROUGH. make verify and the CI doc-helper-flags-check step read its green as
'no instruction document passes a helper a flag it lacks', and nothing
downstream re-derives that. A blind version prints the same ok line while a
driver tells a stuck worker to run a command that exits 2 - the #1835 state.
THE CASES ARE MINIATURE TREES (--root): a fixture mailbox helper that accepts
--to/--from/--body, and one template. The BAD pair covers the single-line form
and the backslash-continued form most real invocations take. The GOOD case holds
the shapes a naive extractor gets wrong: flags inside a $(...) substitution, a
flag after a pipe, a .sh wrapper handing off to a .py parser that builds its
option names, and a flag mentioned in prose after an inline span closes.
CHARTER (discussion #1830): the gate must never block a valid command - the GOOD
cases are its purpose controls - and must report a flag the helper lacks - the BAD
cases. #1839 added one shell reader for every question the gate asks, with one case
per shape the earlier three hand-written readers disagreed on.
#1842 taught the reader that an unescaped backtick opens a nested command inside a
fence, and added one BAD case (the shape it missed) and one GOOD case (the prose
span edges and closing backtick the new nesting must not misread).
#1844 bounded that reader: a backtick substitution holding a backslash or # is
not read but counted as unchecked, so the GOOD case holds those shapes too.

cases.name: bad-unknown-flag
cases.why: The #1835 shape on one line: an escalation command passing --kind to a mailbox whose parser rejects it. If this scores GOOD the gate cannot see the defect it was written for.

cases.name: bad-continuation-line
cases.why: The same unknown flag on a backslash-continued line. Most multi-line helper invocations in the command documents take this shape; a gate reading one physical line would pass it.

cases.name: bad-flag-after-quoted-separator
cases.why: The unknown flag sits after a quoted argument holding '#' and ';'. The first cut of the gate split at punctuation without reading quotes and passed this; counter-model review found it. If it scores GOOD, any quoted message with a hash or semicolon hides every flag after it.

cases.name: bad-quoted-option-value
cases.why: An unknown option written as --kind="message". The second cut of the gate dropped any word with a quoted part, so quoting the value hid the option; counter-model review found it. If this scores GOOD, quoting a value is a way past the gate.

cases.name: bad-paren-quoted-in-substitution
cases.why: The unknown flag follows "$(printf '(')". The pre-#1839 reader counted parentheses without reading quotes, never saw the substitution close, swallowed --kind and passed this. If it scores GOOD, a quoted paren in a substitution hides every flag after it.

cases.name: bad-process-substitution
cases.why: The unknown flag follows <(printf x). A reader that opens only $( reads the process substitution's ')' as the end of the command, swallows --kind and passes this (counter-model review on #1839). If it scores GOOD, every flag after a <( or >( is unchecked.

cases.name: bad-comment-after-separator
cases.why: A comment straight after ';' holds an apostrophe and a trailing backslash. A reader that takes ';#' for one word reads the apostrophe as an open quote, the next invocation as message text, and passes its --kind (counter-model review on #1839).

cases.name: bad-option-value-with-substitution
cases.why: --kind=message$(printf '') passes --kind whatever its value holds. A reader that keeps an option name only when the quote or substitution starts right after '=' drops it and passes this (counter-model review on #1839).

cases.name: bad-comment-backtick-before-invocation
cases.why: A comment with a backtick, an apostrophe and a trailing backslash precedes an invocation with an unknown flag. A reader that guesses the command start backwards (across the backslash, after the last backtick) reads the apostrophe as a quote and passes --kind (counter-model review on #1839). Inside a fence the gate reads forward from the fence.

cases.name: bad-backtick-in-double-quote
cases.why: Issue #1842: X="`helper --kind m`". A backtick inside double quotes still runs a command, as $( does; the #1839 reader opened a nested command on $( only, so it read the helper as message text and passed --kind. If this scores GOOD, a backtick substitution in a quoted assignment hides every flag on the helper inside it.

cases.name: good-known-flags
cases.why: THE HALF THAT MATTERS for a gate in make verify: every shape the live documents use that a naive extractor misreads - substitution, pipe, delegated parser with computed option names, prose after an inline span. A gate that flags any of them blocks every merge. It also holds a quoted --body whose TEXT contains --kind, '#' and ';': reading quoted text as flags would block a valid command over its message wording. And a helper path inside a quoted --body: read as an invocation, its message text would block verify.

cases.name: good-flag-after-helper-substitution
cases.why: PURPOSE CONTROL: the helper runs inside $(...) and --kind belongs to the outer echo, after the substitution closes. The pre-#1839 reader read past the helper's own ')' and blocked this valid command.

cases.name: good-quote-continued-across-lines
cases.why: PURPOSE CONTROL: a quoted --body continued with a backslash onto a line holding a helper path. That path is message text. The pre-#1839 reader restarted quote state at each physical line, read it as a second invocation and blocked this valid command.

cases.name: good-escaped-backtick-in-continued-quote
cases.why: PURPOSE CONTROL: a quoted --body with escaped backticks, continued onto a line holding a helper path. That path is message text. A reader that takes the escaped backtick for a code-span edge drops the opening quote and blocks this valid command (counter-model review on #1839).

cases.name: good-helper-path-in-comment
cases.why: PURPOSE CONTROL: a shell comment names a helper with a flag it lacks. A commented command never runs. A reader that counts a path inside a comment as an invocation blocks this valid document (counter-model review on #1839).

cases.name: good-comment-quote-before-message
cases.why: PURPOSE CONTROL: the same comment shape with a double quote, before a --body that names a helper as message text. A reader that starts after the comment's backtick pairs the comment's quote with the --body quote and blocks this valid document on the message text (counter-model review on #1839).

cases.name: good-inline-spans-near-backticks
cases.why: THE HALF THAT MATTERS for #1842's change: backticks are also Markdown code-span edges. In prose a later span holding --kind must not be read as the helper's flag; in a fence the closing backtick ends the helper's command, so a flag after it belongs to the outer echo; and an escaped backtick in double quotes stays message text. It also holds backtick substitutions with a backslash or '#' (#1844), which the gate counts as unchecked instead of reading: an escaped quote inside one, a comment, and a comment straight after a subshell. Reading any of these as an invocation's flag would block valid documents in make verify.

anchors.why: CONSTRUCTED: the gate is new. This is the weaker check the obvious framing produces - confirm each named helper exists. It misses both BAD cases, where the helper exists and the flag does not, and agrees with the gate on the GOOD case.
